    How the communications department is discouraging overreliance on AI

    By Tripp HendersonSeptember 3, 2026 Baylor News No Comments3 Mins Read
    Midland freshman Adalise Thompson, Garden Grove, California, freshman Jacob Hansen and Jacksonville, Florida, freshman Logan Thigpen communicate with ChatGPT. The art of communication is changing due to artificial intelligence. Hannah Webb | News Editor
    Share
    Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Email

    By Tripp Henderson | Staff Writer

    Listen to audio version of this article
    Sponsored by
    0:00 / 3:23
    Instaread

    As artificial intelligence advances, it is fundamentally changing how humans communicate. Amid these changes, the university’s communications department is emphasizing AI as a “tool” to maximize efficiency while avoiding overreliance.

    Dr. Jacob S. Ford, a professor in the communications department, implemented a course called Communications and New Technology. The course provides an overview of communications research and technology, and class discussions do not shy away from some of the harder questions about AI.

    “We really focus in on [AI] and talk about how communicating with AI might start to shape and alter our communication,” Ford said. “And then, as we interact with AI, how does that alter our communication with others?”

    As more research comes out on AI, Ford and his students discuss those studies and how to interact with AI ethically. Ford said it is important for students to use artificial intelligence as a tool, but not to let it replace critical thinking.

    Ford said that AI can be used effectively to “automate something that’s not consequential to you thinking deeply or processing or thinking critically about the topic that you’re studying.”

    Dr. Ashley K. Barrett from the communications department said that AI can be used in “a beneficial way and ethical way, or can be a tool that we use more in a non-virtuous way,” but that Baylor has the ability to “ figure out what that means and how that manifests at a Christian-based university.”

    Barrett said AI is helpful in many ways, like fixing grammar and punctuation in emails, but human involvement is still important to preserve communication.

    “You have to be able to use AI as a co-author, but you have to remain the author of your identity,” Barrett said.

    Barrett said that AI is sometimes used to create “imagined conversations.” These are chats with AI that simulate a social interaction to prepare the individual for the real conversation.

    While Barrett recognizes that these chats can help you express yourself and build confidence, she said an AI agent’s predicted conversation may not translate to reality because it does not understand the “storied history” of your relationships and “only has the context that you give it.”

    Additionally, Ford is concerned that students will replace human interaction with AI companionship. A new study by Common Sense Media shows that three in four students have used AI companions, and research by the Center for Democracy and Technology found that 42% have used AI for friendship and 19% for romantic relationships.

    “I’m just concerned that it’s going to push students away from each other,” Ford said. “They feel like they have a friend online that just talks to them all the time, that tells them what they want to hear and so they don’t need social interaction as much.”

    Ford also warned about the danger of relying on artificial intelligence and likened it to the addictive nature of social media.

    “Put some barriers on the [AI] applications you’re using and how much time is on them,” Ford said. “Be aware that they might be designed in a way to keep you on there.”

    Barrett echoed similar concerns about AI dependence

    “If we over-rely on something, then we’ll face repercussions of that down the road, and we’ll lose what makes us human and connecting with others,” she said.

    As AI becomes more prevalent in academia, Barrett emphasizes using it alongside good ethics.

    “Everyone’s going to eventually build proficiencies in AI … and that necessitates that we use it morally, we use it ethically, we use it virtuously,” Barrett said.

    Baylor cross country brings confidence and experience into season

    By Aidan O'ConnorSeptember 3, 2026Updated:September 3, 2026 Cross Country and Track & Field No Comments3 Mins Read
    Junior Ruth Kimeli jumps ahead of a competing runner at the Arturio Barrios Invite in College Station. Photo courtesy of Baylor Athletics
    Share
    Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Email

    By Aidan O’Connor | Sports Writer

    Confidence and experience are the backbone of champions and Baylor cross country believes it has both in spades.

    “With experience, you have a lot more consistency,” head coach David Barnett said. “There’s a big gap between your best race and your second best race. I’m definitely excited to see the upperclassmen step in and put it out there. I think the underclassmen will definitely follow their lead.”

    One of the biggest changes for the Bears is the mentality they are bringing into this year.

    “Last year, sometimes we weren’t as confident in what we can do,” senior Mackenize Browne said. “This year, I feel like we came back from the summer training with a great mindset, wanting to get at it and wanting to have better goals.”

    The change in confidence has shown in the team’s practices leading into the season. The Bears have grown to support each other improve every day.

    “Working together last year, it was uneasy,” Browne said. “This year, we grew to use each other to help each other get better. In the workouts, they just show because the workouts have been way better, the teamwork has been amazing.”

    The Bears have 18 upperclassmen in total between the men and women’s teams coming into this season.

    The men’s team has its No. 1 in junior Jack Sterrett and No. 2 runner in senior Straton Miller returning. Baylor believes it has the potential to go above and beyond this season with the experience gained from 2025.

    “Jack’s probably our top guy, but we have a couple other guys that are in a similar situation,” Barnett said. “A couple years ago, we had a couple guys that were all-region. I think this year we have a couple seniors that are in a position they can do the same type of thing.”

    Baylor looks to making noise nationally if its leaders consistently finish at the top.

    “If you can get a couple guys that are all-region, all of a sudden you have a really good opportunity to have a good team,” Barnett said.

    The women’s side sees the return of two-time South Central All-Region honoree junior Ruth Kimeli, who finished in the top 10 twice at the Arturio Barrios Invitational in College Station and at the NCAA South Central Region. Browne also makes her comeback after she went through a season ending heart surgery last year. Senior Eastern Kentucky transfer Khadijah Ennasri brings two individual wins at the Asbury and EKU invitationals in 2025.

    With all of the depth and talent across the board, the women’s team looks to be one of the strongest in Barnett’s tenure with the Bears.

    “On paper, it’s definitely the best,” Barnett said. “Top three as far as track time is concerned. Anytime you have national qualifiers coming back, that’s a big deal.”

    Baylor takes its confidence and experience into their 2026 campaign on Friday at the Aggie Opener at the Watts Cross Country Course in College Station.
